findings.text: The instruction attribute table encodes prefix families as small integers: conventional REX family uses twelve, two-byte VEX uses thirteen, three-byte VEX uses fourteen, EVEX uses fifteen, REX2 uses sixteen, and XOP uses seventeen.
Legacy prefix handling caps the last-prefix count at three and the legacy-group prefix count at eleven.
Immediate operand size is encoded one through seven meaning byte, word, doubleword, quadword, pointer, thirty-two-bit variable word, and natural variable word respectively.

A single attribute word packs four small numeric fields low to high followed by flag bits: prefix occupies offset zero width five, escape follows width two, group follows width five, immediate follows width three, and individual feature flags start immediately above. Each numeric field also defines a width, an all-ones maximum, and a shifted mask.

Feature flags are single bits counted upward from the flag base: ModRM presence first, then forced sixty-four-bit, second immediate, memory offset, variant, VEX-or-XOP acceptance, VEX-only, EVEX-only, REX2 prohibition, REX2 variant, EVEX scalable, and sixty-four-bit invalid last. VEX and XOP acceptance share the same bit.
Three constructors place raw escape, group, and immediate numbers into their attribute positions, with the group constructor additionally marking ModRM as required.
Segment override tracking uses zero for ignore, one for default, and two through seven for code, stack, data, extra, FS, and GS respectively.
Decoded instruction data uses a thirty-two-bit unsigned type for attribute words, an eight-bit unsigned type for raw bytes, and a signed integer type for decoded numeric values.

Early mapping setup is parameterized by a record holding a page-table page allocator callback and its release callback, an opaque context passed to allocation, a page flag for upper-level entries, an identity-mapping offset, a boolean enabling one-gigabyte pages, and a kernel page-table flag override.
Memory-mapped I/O instruction classification distinguishes decode failure, plain write, immediate write, plain read, zero-extending read, sign-extending read, and string move.

Each decoded field records its length in bytes and a flag that becomes nonzero once its accessor has run. One configuration stores either a signed value or up to four raw bytes; the alternate configuration stores a signed value plus a union of a little-endian view and four raw bytes.

A decoded instruction aggregates prefix, REX, a VEX-or-XOP slot, opcode, ModRM, SIB, displacement, and two trailing slots where the first selects among immediate and sixty-four-bit move offsets and the second selects between a second move offset and a second immediate, followed by emulated-prefix length, attribute word, operand and address widths, total length, a sixty-four-bit mode marker, and three kernel pointers marking start, buffer end, and next unconsumed byte.
The maximum architectural instruction length accepted by the decoder is fifteen bytes.

Extension-byte predicates test single bits: REX2 checks values sixty-four, thirty-two, and sixteen for its three extensions, VEX checks values one-hundred-twenty-eight, sixty-four, thirty-two, and four for register extensions and length, two-byte VEX fixes its map selector at one, the vector selector comes from a middle field shifted down by three, and three-byte VEX map values cap at thirty-one.

XOP decoding tests register extensions with values one-hundred-twenty-eight, sixty-four, and thirty-two in its second byte, and tests operand size, vector selector, and length with value one-hundred-twenty-eight, a middle field, and value four in its third byte, while its map selector is constrained to the inclusive range eight to thirty-one.
Decode mode selects thirty-two-bit, sixty-four-bit, or current kernel build, with a count marker terminating the enumeration.
A kernel convenience entry decodes the instruction at a given pointer using the maximum length bound and the kernel-build mode.
Attribute retrieval is defined as ensuring the ModRM field has been fetched.
XOP classification returns false unless an AVX-or-XOP indication is present and a further AVX helper confirms XOP; a separate predicate reports whether any emulated-prefix bytes were consumed.

Byte offsets of successive fields are computed cumulatively: REX starts after legacy prefixes, each later field starts after the accumulated lengths of all earlier fields through displacement to immediate.
Two opcodes receive special handling: decimal thirty-one for popping the stack segment and decimal one-hundred-forty-two for moving segment registers.

An interrupt-masking hazard is reported for a stack-segment pop or for a segment-register move whose register selector equals two denoting the stack segment, since both defer debug-exception delivery.
Register classification uses zero for thirty-two-bit, one for sixty-four-bit, and one hundred as the invalid sentinel for both number and type.
Each header is protected against multiple inclusion by defining its own include-guard macro on first processing.

Intel processor identities combine vendor, family, and model into one token via a maker macro; a wildcard identity matches any family and model, family five covers early Pentium and Quark parts, family six model two-hundred-fifty-five marks the end of family six, and family fifteen covers Pentium Four variants.

Family-six big-core identities each pair family six with a distinct model byte, progressing from Pentium Pro era through Core, Nehalem, Westmere, Sandy Bridge, Ivy Bridge, Haswell, Broadwell, Skylake including Kaby Lake and Comet Lake variants, Cannon Lake, Ice Lake server and client forms, Rocket Lake, Tiger Lake, Sapphire and Emerald Rapids, Granite Rapids, and Bartlett Lake, with Diamond Rapids placed in family nineteen model one.

Hybrid and low-power identities each pair a family with a distinct model byte, covering Lakefield, Alder Lake, Raptor Lake, Meteor Lake, Arrow Lake, Lunar Lake, Panther Lake, and Wildcat Lake in family six, Nova Lake in family eighteen, Atom Bonnell through Darkmont generations in family six, and Knights Landing and Knights Mill many-core parts in family six.
Coarse CPU type uses thirty-two for Atom and sixty-four for Core with zero meaning unknown; native-efficient-core identifiers use two for Crestmont and three for Skymont.
Mid-platform power state encoding places the logical substate at bit offset four and marks its type with the eighth bit.

Branch-trace and precise-event buffers each span sixteen pages, with the precise-event threshold for multiple records derived from usable space divided by record stride and single-record threshold fixed at one; event capacity is eight for format four, thirty-two general plus sixteen fixed otherwise, with a mask covering the general range.

The debug store is page-aligned and holds paired base, index, absolute-maximum, and interrupt-threshold counters for branch tracing then for precise events, followed by a reset-value array sized for all general plus fixed counters; a companion structure provides contiguous byte areas for both buffers sized by their respective capacities.

Processor-trace capability discovery uses two CPUID leaves of four registers each and enumerates features from maximum subleaf through filtering, timing, tracing, and output options ending with period and threshold tables.
When tracing support is unavailable the header supplies inert replacements that perform no stop action and report zero or false for capability validation and event classification.

Inter-processor messaging to the power unit distinguishes BIOS, graphics-driver, ISP-driver, and reserved channels numbered zero to three, shifts the channel by six to form command bases, and masks command type with the reserved value shifted likewise.

Decoding proceeds field by field from undecoded to decoded as marked by each field flag; offsets and later fields become meaningful only after earlier lengths are known, and attribute completion depends on ModRM retrieval.
